i skole.explanation: "I skole" means "in school". To say you are going there, use "skal" (am going to): "Jeg skal i skole" (I am off to school). To say you attend school as a pupil, use "at gå" (to go): "Hun går i skole i Odense" (She goes to school in Odense).

i stedet.explanation: "I stedet" means "instead". To say which thing you pick in place of something just mentioned, put it at the end: "Vi tager bussen i stedet" (We take the bus instead). To say instead of what, use "i stedet for" (instead of): "Jeg vil have te i stedet for kaffe" (I want tea instead of coffee).

i stedet for.explanation: "I stedet for" means "instead of". Literally, it is "in the place for". To say you choose one thing and not another, say: "Jeg vil have te i stedet for kaffe" (I want tea instead of coffee). To say instead of doing something, add "at" (to) before the verb: "i stedet for at vente" (instead of waiting).

i stykker.explanation: "I stykker" means "broken". Literally, it is "in pieces". To say something has stopped working, use "er" (is): "Min cykel er i stykker" (My bike is broken). To say something broke, use "gik" (went): "Telefonen gik i stykker" (The phone broke).

i tide.explanation: "I tide" means "in time". To say you finished before a deadline, say: "Jeg afleverede opgaven i tide" (I handed in the assignment in time). Do not mix it up with "til tiden" (on time), which means at the agreed time: "Toget kom til tiden" (The train came on time).

i tilfælde af.explanation: "I tilfælde af" means "in case of". It is built from "i" (in), "et tilfælde" (a case) and "af" (of). To warn about something that might happen, say: "i tilfælde af brand" (in case of fire). To follow it with a whole sentence, add "at" (that): "Tag en paraply med i tilfælde af at det regner" (Bring an umbrella in case it rains).

i udlandet.explanation: "I udlandet" means "abroad". To say where you live, put "i" (in) before it: "Jeg bor i udlandet" (I live abroad). To say where you are going, use "til" (to): "Jeg rejser til udlandet" (I am traveling abroad). To say where someone comes from, use "fra" (from): "Han kommer fra udlandet" (He comes from abroad).

i virkeligheden.explanation: "I virkeligheden" means "in reality". It is built from "i" (in) and "virkeligheden" (the reality). To say the truth differs from how things look, say: "Det ser nemt ud, men i virkeligheden er det svært" (It looks easy, but in reality it is hard).

i weekenden.explanation: "I weekenden" means "this weekend / on the weekend". To talk about the coming weekend, say: "Vi skal i biografen i weekenden" (We are going to the movies this weekend). To talk about the weekend just gone, use the past tense: "Jeg var i Aarhus i weekenden" (I was in Aarhus last weekend). To say how you spend every weekend, say: "Jeg sover længe i weekenden" (I sleep late on weekends).

i år.explanation: "I år" means "this year". Literally, it is "in year". To say something repeats each year, use "hvert år" (every year): "Vi rejser hvert år" (We travel every year).

i øvrigt.explanation: "I øvrigt" means "by the way". To add a side remark about something already said, say: "Bogen er god. Den er i øvrigt billig." (The book is good. It is also cheap, by the way.)

iblandt.explanation: "Iblandt" means "among". It is built from "i" (in) and "blandt" (among). The shorter word "blandt" means the same: "Hun er blandt de bedste" (She is among the best).

ideel.explanation: "Ideel" means "ideal". The noun is "et ideal" (an ideal). To say something is perfect for a purpose, add "til" (for) and the purpose: "Huset er ideelt til en stor familie" (The house is ideal for a big family).

identisk.explanation: "Identisk" means "identical". To say two things are exactly the same, add "med" (with) and the other thing: "Svaret er identisk med mit" (The answer is identical to mine). The Danish word ends in "-isk", not "-ical".

idet.explanation: "Idet" means "as". Literally, it is "i det" (in that), written as one word. To say two things happen at the same moment, say: "Idet han gik ud, slukkede han lyset" (As he went out, he turned off the light).

idræt.explanation: "Idræt" means "PE". To say what class you have at school, say: "Vi har idræt efter frokost" (We have PE after lunch). Outside school, it means "sports" as an activity: "Hun elsker idræt" (She loves sports).

ifølge.explanation: "Ifølge" means "according to". To name where the information comes from, say: "ifølge lægen" (according to the doctor). To give your own view instead, use "efter min mening" (in my opinion): "Efter min mening er filmen dårlig" (In my opinion the film is bad).

igen.explanation: "Igen" means "again". To say you will return, say: "Jeg kommer igen" (I will come back). To say another person is included, use "også" (too): "Jeg kommer også" (I am coming too).

igennem.explanation: "Igennem" means "through". The shorter word "gennem" means the same: "gennem skoven" (through the forest). To say you read or check something from start to finish, put "igennem" after the verb: "Jeg læste bogen igennem" (I read the book all the way through).

ikke.explanation: "Ikke" means "not". To say something is not so, put it after "er" (is): "Det er ikke dyrt" (It is not expensive). Do not mix it up with "nej" (no), which answers a question: "Nej, jeg er ikke sulten" (No, I am not hungry).

ikke desto mindre.explanation: "Ikke desto mindre" means "nevertheless". Literally, it is "not the less". To say something is still true despite what was just said, say: "Det var dyrt. Ikke desto mindre købte vi det" (It was expensive. Nevertheless, we bought it).

ikke endnu.explanation: "Ikke endnu" means "not yet". To answer a question about being ready, say: "Er du klar?" "Ikke endnu." (Are you ready? Not yet.) To say you have not done something so far, put "endnu" (yet) at the end: "Jeg har ikke ringet endnu" (I have not called yet). Do not mix it up with "ikke mere" (not anymore), which says something has stopped: "Jeg bor ikke her mere" (I do not live here anymore).

ikke engang.explanation: "Ikke engang" means "not even". To say something is missing although you would expect it, say: "Hun har ikke engang tid til en kop kaffe" (She does not even have time for a cup of coffee). The part "engang" also appears in the fairy-tale opening "Der var engang" (Once upon a time).

ikke mere.explanation: "Ikke mere" means "no more". To turn down more of something, say: "Mere kaffe?" "Nej tak, ikke mere." (More coffee? No thank you, no more.) To say something has stopped, it means "not anymore": "Jeg bor ikke her mere" (I do not live here anymore).

ild.explanation: "Ild" means "fire", as in flames. Do not mix it up with "en brand" (a destructive fire): "Der er brand i huset" (The house is on fire). To ask someone for a light, say: "Har du ild?" (Do you have a light?)
